The largest aircraft carrier in the world is named after **Gerald R. Ford**, the 38th President of the United States (1974–1977).

Its full designation is the **USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN-78)**, which is the lead ship of the Ford-class of nuclear-powered supercarriers for the United States Navy. The vessel has a displacement of about 100,000 long tons at full load, making it one of the largest warships ever constructed.

**USS _Gerald R. Ford_ (CVN-78)** is an aircraft carrier of the United States Navy and the lead ship of her class. The ship is named after the 38th president of the United States, Gerald Ford, whose World War II naval service included combat duty aboard the light aircraft carrier_Monterey_ in the Pacific Theater.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Gerald_R._Ford#cite_note-16)
Construction began on 11 August 2005, when Northrop Grumman held a ceremonial steel cut for a 15-ton plate that forms part of a side shell unit of the carrier. The keel of _Gerald R. Ford_ was laid down on 14 November 2009. She was christened on 9 November 2013.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Gerald_R._Ford#cite_note-NavyLiveChristening-5)_Gerald R. Ford_ entered the fleet, replacing the decommissioned USS _Enterprise_(CVN-65), which ended her 51 years of active service in December 2012.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Gerald_R._Ford#cite_note-NavyCVN21Issues-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Gerald_R._Ford#cite_note-18)
Originally scheduled for delivery in 2015, _Gerald R. Ford_ was delivered to the Navy on 31 May 2017 and formally commissioned by President Donald Trump on 22 July 2017. She departed Naval Station Norfolk on her first deployment on 2 May 2023. When she was commissioned she was the world's largest aircraft carrier and the largest warship ever constructed.

The **_Gerald R. Ford_-class**aircraft carrier is a class of nuclear-powered aircraft carriers built for the United States Navy to replace portions of the aging _Nimitz_-class carrier fleet. Named after former U.S. president Gerald R. Ford,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_R._Ford-class_aircraft_carrier#cite_note-15) the class is designed to provide upgraded weapons systems, improved energy efficiency, reduced operating costs, and reduced crew requirements. Key changes include the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS), Advanced Arresting Gear (AAG), and a redesigned flight deck.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_R._Ford-class_aircraft_carrier#cite_note-CVN_21-16) The lead ship, USS _Gerald R. Ford_, was commissioned in 2017 with the second ship of the class, USS _John F. Kennedy_, expected to be delivered in 2027.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_R._Ford-class_aircraft_carrier#cite_note-17)

# Taking the Seas: The Rise of the American Aircraft Carrier
### Introduction
The USS _Gerald R. Ford_(CVN 78) launched in 2017 as the largest, most powerful warship the world had ever seen - ten times larger than the USS _Langley_(CV 1), America's first aircraft carrier. The _Ford_ defined a new class of these capital ships, more dynamic, more capable than any that has sailed before her. Yet the legacy of her predecessors dating back nearly a century can be seen in her lines and courses through her steel.
This online exhibit explores the history of the American aircraft carrier - from the early 20th century when hydraulic gears launched airplanes made of wood and fabric from decks planked with wood; to the 21st century, when carbon-fiber jets are launched from electric rails.
President Washington believed that with a "decisive naval force," America can do "everything honorable and glorious." Carriers earned glory in the great naval battles of World War II, and in the post-war years proved Theodore Roosevelt's studied observation that, "A good Navy is not a provocation to war..." but "...the surest guarantee of peace." The USS _Gerald R. Ford_, like the _Nimitz_, the _Enterprise_, the _Forrestal_, and the _Essex_, continues this tradition, serving as a primary guarantee of the peaceful, free use of the seas.

# Taking the Seas: The Rise of the American Aircraft Carrier
## Early Carriers
* * *
In 1912 Great Britain launched the first airplane from the deck of a moving ship, and Japan launched sea planes in air raids as early as 1914. Within four years, the British converted an ocean liner to a flattop carrier of aircraft whose primary purpose was to launch and land airplanes at sea.
By 1922 the United States converted a coaling ship into its first aircraft carrier. The USS _Langley_(CV-1) was soon followed by the _Lexington_ and _Saratoga_, two converted cruisers. With these three vessels, America was keeping pace not only with Great Britain, but also with Japan, whose navy covered the western Pacific Ocean.
Between the great wars, these three naval powers joined Italy and France to try to limit the size and cost of their fleets. They signed the Washington Treaty in 1922, restricting the tonnage of the battleships, which were still seen as the primary ship of all navies. But carriers, too, were limited by the treaty. The Washington Treaty would survive unchallenged for twelve years. The United States began building the bigger carriers by 1937, and used them in 1941 after the attack on Pearl Harbor.

**USS _Gerald R. Ford_ (CVN-78)** is an aircraft carrier of the United States Navy and the lead ship of her class. The ship is named after the 38th president of the United States, Gerald Ford, whose World War II naval service included combat duty aboard the light aircraft carrier_Monterey_ in the Pacific Theater.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Gerald_R._Ford#cite_note-16)
Construction began on 11 August 2005, when Northrop Grumman held a ceremonial steel cut for a 15-ton plate that forms part of a side shell unit of the carrier. The keel of _Gerald R. Ford_ was laid down on 14 November 2009. She was christened on 9 November 2013.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Gerald_R._Ford#cite_note-NavyLiveChristening-5)_Gerald R. Ford_ entered the fleet, replacing the decommissioned USS _Enterprise_(CVN-65), which ended her 51 years of active service in December 2012.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Gerald_R._Ford#cite_note-NavyCVN21Issues-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Gerald_R._Ford#cite_note-18)
Originally scheduled for delivery in 2015, _Gerald R. Ford_ was delivered to the Navy on 31 May 2017 and formally commissioned by President Donald Trump on 22 July 2017. She departed Naval Station Norfolk on her first deployment on 2 May 2023. When she was commissioned she was the world's largest aircraft carrier and the largest warship ever constructed.

# Taking the Seas: The Rise of the American Aircraft Carrier
### Introduction
The USS _Gerald R. Ford_(CVN 78) launched in 2017 as the largest, most powerful warship the world had ever seen - ten times larger than the USS _Langley_(CV 1), America's first aircraft carrier. The _Ford_ defined a new class of these capital ships, more dynamic, more capable than any that has sailed before her. Yet the legacy of her predecessors dating back nearly a century can be seen in her lines and courses through her steel.
This online exhibit explores the history of the American aircraft carrier - from the early 20th century when hydraulic gears launched airplanes made of wood and fabric from decks planked with wood; to the 21st century, when carbon-fiber jets are launched from electric rails.
President Washington believed that with a "decisive naval force," America can do "everything honorable and glorious." Carriers earned glory in the great naval battles of World War II, and in the post-war years proved Theodore Roosevelt's studied observation that, "A good Navy is not a provocation to war..." but "...the surest guarantee of peace." The USS _Gerald R. Ford_, like the _Nimitz_, the _Enterprise_, the _Forrestal_, and the _Essex_, continues this tradition, serving as a primary guarantee of the peaceful, free use of the seas.

# Taking the Seas: The Rise of the American Aircraft Carrier
## Early Carriers
* * *
In 1912 Great Britain launched the first airplane from the deck of a moving ship, and Japan launched sea planes in air raids as early as 1914. Within four years, the British converted an ocean liner to a flattop carrier of aircraft whose primary purpose was to launch and land airplanes at sea.
By 1922 the United States converted a coaling ship into its first aircraft carrier. The USS _Langley_(CV-1) was soon followed by the _Lexington_ and _Saratoga_, two converted cruisers. With these three vessels, America was keeping pace not only with Great Britain, but also with Japan, whose navy covered the western Pacific Ocean.
Between the great wars, these three naval powers joined Italy and France to try to limit the size and cost of their fleets. They signed the Washington Treaty in 1922, restricting the tonnage of the battleships, which were still seen as the primary ship of all navies. But carriers, too, were limited by the treaty. The Washington Treaty would survive unchallenged for twelve years. The United States began building the bigger carriers by 1937, and used them in 1941 after the attack on Pearl Harbor.

**USS _Gerald R. Ford_ (CVN-78)** is an aircraft carrier of the United States Navy and the lead ship of her class. The ship is named after the 38th president of the United States, Gerald Ford, whose World War II naval service included combat duty aboard the light aircraft carrier_Monterey_ in the Pacific Theater.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Gerald_R._Ford#cite_note-16)

Ford_ entered the fleet, replacing the decommissioned USS _Enterprise_(CVN-65), which ended her 51 years of active service in December 2012.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Gerald_R._Ford#cite_note-NavyCVN21Issues-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Gerald_R._Ford#cite_note-18)
Originally scheduled for delivery in 2015, _Gerald R. Ford_ was delivered to the Navy on 31 May 2017 and formally commissioned by President Donald Trump on 22 July 2017. # Taking the Seas: The Rise of the American Aircraft Carrier
### Introduction
The USS _Gerald R. Ford_(CVN 78) launched in 2017 as the largest, most powerful warship the world had ever seen - ten times larger than the USS _Langley_(CV 1), America's first aircraft carrier. The _Ford_ defined a new class of these capital ships, more dynamic, more capable than any that has sailed before her. Yet the legacy of her predecessors dating back nearly a century can be seen in her lines and courses through her steel.
This online exhibit explores the history of the American aircraft carrier - from the early 20th century when hydraulic gears launched airplanes made of wood and fabric from decks planked with wood; to the 21st century, when carbon-fiber jets are launched from electric rails.
President Washington believed that with a "decisive naval force," America can do "everything honorable and glorious." Carriers earned glory in the great naval battles of World War II, and in the post-war years proved Theodore Roosevelt's studied observation that, "A good Navy is not a provocation to war..." but "...the surest guarantee of peace." The USS _Gerald R. Ford_, like the _Nimitz_, the _Enterprise_, the _Forrestal_, and the _Essex_, continues this tradition, serving as a primary guarantee of the peaceful, free use of the seas.

# Taking the Seas: The Rise of the American Aircraft Carrier
## Early Carriers
* * *
In 1912 Great Britain launched the first airplane from the deck of a moving ship, and Japan launched sea planes in air raids as early as 1914. Within four years, the British converted an ocean liner to a flattop carrier of aircraft whose primary purpose was to launch and land airplanes at sea.
By 1922 the United States converted a coaling ship into its first aircraft carrier. The USS _Langley_(CV-1) was soon followed by the _Lexington_ and _Saratoga_, two converted cruisers. With these three vessels, America was keeping pace not only with Great Britain, but also with Japan, whose navy covered the western Pacific Ocean.
Between the great wars, these three naval powers joined Italy and France to try to limit the size and cost of their fleets. They signed the Washington Treaty in 1922, restricting the tonnage of the battleships, which were still seen as the primary ship of all navies. But carriers, too, were limited by the treaty. The Washington Treaty would survive unchallenged for twelve years. The United States began building the bigger carriers by 1937, and used them in 1941 after the attack on Pearl Harbor.

The largest aircraft carrier in the world is named after **Gerald R. Ford**, the 38th President of the United States (1974–1977).

Its full designation is the **USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN-78)**, which is the lead ship of the Ford-class of nuclear-powered supercarriers for the United States Navy. The vessel has a displacement of about 100,000 long tons at full load, making it one of the largest warships ever constructed.
